Fast rule: Find the year’s Doomsday, then use a nearby anchor date from the reference.

The Doomsday algorithm

Three small pieces, then count to a familiar date.

Every year has a weekday shared by a memorable set of dates—its “Doomsday.” The method works for Gregorian dates from 1583 onward.

1

Century anchor

For 1800s/2200s use Friday; 1900s/2300s Wednesday; 2000s/2400s Tuesday; 2100s/2500s Sunday. The pattern moves back two days every century.

2

Year anchor

Take the last two digits of the year. Divide by 12, add the remainder, then add remainder ÷ 4 (whole number). Move forward that many days from the century anchor.

y/12 + (y mod 12) + floor((y mod 12)/4)
3

Nearest Doomsday

Find the month’s anchor date below. Count forward or backward to your date, wrapping weekdays as needed. In leap years, Jan/Feb anchors shift back one day.

Month anchor dates

All of these fall on that year’s Doomsday.

January 3*
February 28*
March 14
April 4
May 9
June 6
July 11
August 8
September 5
October 10
November 7
December 12

* In a leap year, use Jan 4 and Feb 29 instead.

Century anchors

CenturyAnchor weekday
1600, 2000, 2400…Tuesday
1700, 2100, 2500…Sunday
1800, 2200, 2600…Friday
1900, 2300, 2700…Wednesday

Leap year: divisible by 4, except century years unless divisible by 400.

Worked example: July 20, 1969

The 1900s anchor is Wednesday. For 69: 69÷12 = 5 remainder 9; add 5 + 9 + 2 = 16. Wednesday + 16 = Friday, so 1969’s Doomsday is Friday. July 11 is a Doomsday; nine days later, July 20, is Sunday.

Quick memory hooks

“I work 9 to 5 at 7‑11”: May 9, September 5, July 11, November 7. Even months pair: 4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10, 12/12. Pi Day (3/14) is another anchor.
